subject: math

unit.title: Calculation: add, subtract, multiply, divide
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we add and take away bigger numbers, and what does 'lots of' mean?

title: Subtracting two-digit numbers (with exchange)
objectives: By the end, I can subtract two-digit numbers, exchanging a ten for ten ones when the ones are too small.

vocabulary.definition: remove an amount and see what is left
break one ten into ten ones
when the ones you must take away outnumber the ones you have
vocabulary.example: taking 8 ones when you only have 3

emphasize: When there aren't enough ones to take away, BREAK ONE TEN into ten ones — never flip to smaller-from-larger.
Pre-empt the flip error: '7 − 2 because you can't do 2 − 7' (giving 63 − 28 = 45).
Repeat the anchor phrase: 'Not enough ones? Break a ten.'

keyConcepts: exchanging a ten for ten ones
deciding whether an exchange is needed
misconceptions: the smaller-from-larger flip: doing 8 − 3 instead of breaking a ten (63 − 28 = 45)
breaking a ten but forgetting the tens went down by one
adding instead of subtracting when the story says 'spent'
hooks: You had 63p and spent 28p — how much is left?
priorKnowledge: the exchange idea from addition (Lesson 6, reversed)

digital: virtual rods and cubes on the whiteboard block (animated ten-breaking)

video.watchTask: Every time Mr. J breaks a ten into ten ones, shout 'BREAK THE TEN!' — and check that his tens go down by one.

afterCheck.question: When did Mr. J have to break a ten?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: When there weren't enough ones to take away.

plan.goal: Set the pocket-money problem (63p − 28p) and connect to yesterday's exchange, reversed.
plan.note: Tease the problem in the ones — don't solve it yet.
plan.successCriteria: Child predicts something like 'break a ten into ten ones' when asked what today's swap might be.

script.say: You had 63p jingling in your pocket, and you spent 28p on a snack. How much is left? We'll build 63 and take 28 away — but watch out, we're going to hit a problem in the ones! Remember last lesson we traded ten ones for a ten? Guess what we might do today… the other way round!
script.adaptHints: Swap the snack for something the child would buy. Listen for 'break a ten into ten ones'; if shaky, show a rod and count it as ten cubes.

stuckProtocol: If the reverse-trade idea doesn't come: show one ten-rod and count it out as ten cubes — 'one ten IS ten ones, so we can break it open.'

plan.goal: Model 63 − 28: not enough ones → break one ten → 63 becomes 50 and 13 → subtract ones then tens → 35.
plan.note: The animated whiteboard acts out breaking the ten. Name the flip error explicitly and forbid it kindly.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the rod burst into ten cubes, hears '63 is now 50 and 13', and hears 'never flip 3 − 8 into 8 − 3'.

script.say: Here's 63 — six tens, three ones. I need to take away 8 ones… but I only have 3! NOT ENOUGH. Now, some people sneakily flip it and do 8 minus 3 — but that changes the question, so we never do that. Instead: BREAK A TEN! Watch — one ten-rod bursts into ten little ones. Now I have 5 tens and 13 ones — still 63, just dressed differently. Take 8 ones from 13… that leaves 5. Take 2 tens from 5 tens… that leaves 3 tens. Thirty and five — 35! You have 35p left.
script.adaptHints: Make the rod-burst dramatic. Repeat the anchor: 'Not enough ones? Break a ten.'

elements.value: the red ten breaks into ten ones →
Not enough ones? Break a ten — never flip 3 − 8!

plan.goal: Shared build of 52 − 27: the child spots 'not enough ones', calls the break, and finishes both columns.
plan.note: 52 → 40 and 12; 12 − 7 = 5; 40 − 20 = 20 → 25. The child drives every decision.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 2 ones isn't enough, renames 52 as 40 and 12, and answers '25'.

script.say: Together now: 52 take away 27. Here's 52 — five tens, two ones. I need to take 7 ones… look at my ones. Are there enough? … No! What do we shout? … BREAK A TEN! One rod bursts open. Now 52 is dressed as 40 and how many ones? … Twelve! Take 7 from 12… and 2 tens from 4 tens… What's left altogether?
script.adaptHints: Pause for each child decision. If they answer '35', ask: 'Did you take 7 from 12 — or sneak a flip?'

blocks.text: Break a ten: 52 becomes 40 and ___ ones.

wrongAnswers.why: flipped 2 − 7 into 7 − 2, or broke the ten but forgot the tens went down
wrongAnswers.remedy: Can you really take 7 from only 2? Break a ten — and check: how many whole tens are LEFT after the break?

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of subtracting
wrongAnswers.remedy: The story says take away — should the number get bigger or smaller than 52?

plan.goal: Independent diagnostic: 63 − 28 (the hook, now solo) — catches the flip and the forgotten ten.
plan.note: This revisits the hook to close the loop. '45' = flip or unreduced tens; '91' = added.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 35 and can point to where the ten was broken.

script.say: Back to your pocket money — solo this time! You had 63p and spent 28p. Build it, break what needs breaking, and type how much is left.
script.adaptHints: After a correct answer, probe: 'Show me where you broke the ten. How many tens were left after?'

wrongAnswers.why: the flip — did 8 − 3 in the ones (or kept 6 tens after breaking one)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Can you take 8 from only 3? Break a ten first — now count: how many whole tens are left, and how many ones?

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of subtracting
wrongAnswers.remedy: You SPENT money — does your pocket grow when you spend? Take 28 away from 63.

plan.goal: Independent subtracting with and WITHOUT the exchange, so breaking a ten is a decision; stretch across a multiple of ten.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Interleave a no-exchange item (57 − 23) so the child checks the ones first every time.
plan.successCriteria: Child solves 3+ subtractions correctly, including one needing no exchange, saying each time whether a ten had to break.

script.say: Practice time, ten-breaker! Some of these need you to break a ten, and some don't. Your first move every time: look at the ones and ask, 'are there enough?'
script.adaptHints: Frame problems as spending the child's favourite things (pocket money, game coins). Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'I think the ones got flipped.'
Go fully concrete — break the ten slowly together on the whiteboard, counting all ten new ones.
One hint: 'Are there enough ones to take away?'
Re-ask a no-exchange version (48 − 25), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states when to break a ten; end on an earned success.
plan.successCriteria: Child says we break a ten 'when there aren't enough ones to take away'.

script.say: Final question, ten-breaker: WHEN do we have to break a ten? … Exactly — when there aren't enough ones to take away. And you stopped yourself doing the sneaky flip and broke a ten instead. That's exactly what strong mathematicians do — they change the ten, never the question.
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: checking the ones first, renaming 63 as 50 + 13, reducing the tens after the break.

block.prompt: 42 − 17: you must take 7 ones but you only have 2. What do you do?
options: Break one ten into ten ones
block.explain: Not enough ones? Break a ten! 42 becomes 30 and 12 — now you can take 7 ones.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Break one ten into ten ones

wrongAnswers.why: the smaller-from-larger flip — changes the question
wrongAnswers.remedy: If you flip, you're answering a DIFFERENT sum. Keep the question the same: where can you get more ones from?

wrongAnswers.why: doesn't know tens can be opened up
wrongAnswers.remedy: One ten IS ten ones in a coat! Break it open — now how many ones do you have?

hints: A ten-rod is just ten ones stuck together.
Get more ones without changing the number — where from?

reteach.say: A ten-rod is like a chocolate bar with ten squares — snap it and you've got ten ones! 42 = 4 tens, 2 ones. Snap one ten: now 3 tens and 12 ones. Still 42, but now taking 7 ones is easy.

block.caption: Break a ten: one rod becomes ten ones

block.prompt: Break a ten! 52 becomes 40 and how many ones?

wrongAnswers.why: broke the ten but didn't add its ten ones to the pile
wrongAnswers.remedy: The broken ten turned into ten new ones — they join your 2. How many now?

wrongAnswers.why: counted only the new ones and forgot the original 2
wrongAnswers.remedy: You already had 2 ones before the break. Ten new ones plus the old 2 makes…?

hints: The broken ten gives you ten NEW ones.
10 new ones + the 2 you had = ?

reteach.say: 52 is 5 tens and 2 ones. Snap one ten open — ten ones pour out and join the 2 already there: 12 ones. And only 4 whole tens are left. 52 = 40 + 12, just wearing a different coat.

wrongAnswers.why: flipped 2 − 7 into 7 − 2, or forgot the tens went down after the break
wrongAnswers.remedy: Are there enough ones to take 7 from 2? Break a ten — then check how many whole tens are left.

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of subtracting
wrongAnswers.remedy: Take away means the answer must be SMALLER than 52. Remove 27 from the blocks.

hints: Check the ones first: can you take 7 from 2?
After the break: 40 and 12. Now subtract each column.

reteach.say: Slow motion: 52 − 27. Ones check: 2 take away 7 — not enough! Break a ten: 52 → 40 + 12. Ones: 12 − 7 = 5. Tens: 40 − 20 = 20. Answer: 25.

wrongAnswers.why: flipped 1 − 6 into 6 − 1
wrongAnswers.remedy: Can you take 6 ones from just 1? That flip changes the question. Break a ten: 71 becomes 60 and 11.

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of subtracting
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're taking away — the answer must be smaller than 71.

hints: Ones check: 1 take away 6 — enough?

reteach.say: 71 − 26. Only 1 one, but I need to take 6 — break a ten! 71 → 60 + 11. Ones: 11 − 6 = 5. Tens: 60 − 20 = 40. Answer: 45.

wrongAnswers.why: flipped 4 − 8 into 8 − 4
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check: can you take 8 ones from 4? Break a ten instead — 84 becomes 70 and 14.

wrongAnswers.why: broke the ten but kept 8 whole tens
wrongAnswers.remedy: You opened one of your tens to make ones — so how many whole tens are left? 8 or 7?

hints: Ones check: 4 take away 8 — enough?
84 → 70 + 14. Now subtract each column.

reteach.say: 84 − 38. Ones: 4 take away 8 — not enough, break a ten! 84 → 70 + 14. Ones: 14 − 8 = 6. Tens: 70 − 30 = 40. Answer: 46. And the tens went from 8 to 7 the moment we broke one — that's the step people forget.

practiceBank.skill: decide whether to break a ten

block.statement: 57 − 23 needs you to break a ten.
block.explain: Ones check: 7 take away 3 — plenty! No break needed. 57 − 23 = 34.

wrongAnswers.why: thinks every two-digit subtraction needs a break
wrongAnswers.remedy: Only break when the ones run short. Check: 7 take away 3 — are there enough?

wrongAnswers.why: judging by the whole number instead of the ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: The tens take care of themselves — only the ONES decide. Look just at 7 and 3.

hints: Check only the ones: 7 take away 3.
Break a ten only when the ones run short.

reteach.say: Breaking a ten is a rescue move — you only call for it when the ones are in trouble. 57 − 23: taking 3 ones from 7 is easy, no rescue needed. Compare 52 − 27: taking 7 from 2 — rescue! Always check the ones first.

practiceBank.skill: decide whether to break a ten

block.prompt: Sort these subtractions: which need you to break a ten?

wrongAnswers.answer: sorted by how big the numbers are
wrongAnswers.why: checked the tens or the whole number instead of the ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: For each one, cover the tens and look ONLY at the ones: can the first ones-digit give away the second?

wrongAnswers.why: flip-checking (compared 2 and 5 in the wrong order)
wrongAnswers.remedy: You HAVE 8 ones and need to give 5. Is 8 enough? Then no break.

hints: Cover the tens — only the ones decide.
Ask each time: can the ones I HAVE give away the ones I must take?

reteach.say: One question sorts them all: are there enough ones? 52 − 27: 2 can't give 7 — break. 57 − 23: 7 can give 3 — no break. 63 − 28: 3 can't give 8 — break. 48 − 25: 8 can give 5 — no break. 71 − 26: 1 can't give 6 — break.

practiceBank.skill: subtract across a multiple of ten (stretch)

wrongAnswers.why: flipped in the ones (did 3 − 0)
wrongAnswers.remedy: You have ZERO ones — can zero give away 3? Break a ten: 70 becomes 60 and 10.

wrongAnswers.why: broke a ten but kept 7 whole tens
wrongAnswers.remedy: One of your 7 tens opened up into ones. How many whole tens are left before you subtract?

hints: 70 has 0 ones — you'll definitely need to break a ten.

reteach.say: 70 is 7 tens and NO ones at all — so to take 3 ones we must break a ten straight away. 70 → 60 + 10. Ones: 10 − 3 = 7. Tens: 60 − 20 = 40. Answer: 47. Zero ones just means the break happens first!

block.prompt: Mia says 52 − 27 = 35, because 'you can't do 2 − 7, so I did 7 − 2.' What went wrong? What's the real answer?
block.sample: She flipped the ones, which changes the question. Break a ten instead: 52 → 40 and 12; 12 − 7 = 5; 40 − 20 = 20. The real answer is 25.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: She flipped 2 − 7 into 7 − 2; she should break a ten (52 → 40 + 12); the real answer is 25

wrongAnswers.why: shares the smaller-from-larger misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Test it with blocks: build 52, take 27 away by breaking a ten. Do you end on 35 or 25?

wrongAnswers.answer: She should have said it can't be done
wrongAnswers.why: doesn't know the rescue move
wrongAnswers.remedy: It CAN be done — the ones just need backup. Where can 2 get ten more ones from?

hints: Flipping answers a different question — which move keeps the question the same?
Check both answers by adding back: 35 + 27 = ? and 25 + 27 = ?

reteach.say: Here's the detective proof: if 52 − 27 = 35, then 35 + 27 should rebuild 52 — but 35 + 27 = 62. Wrong! With the break: 25 + 27 = 52. Perfect. Flipping the ones quietly swaps the question; breaking a ten keeps it honest.

wrongAnswers.why: reduced the tens but didn't pour the ten new ones in
wrongAnswers.remedy: The broken ten didn't vanish — its ten ones join your 3. How many ones now?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the new ones but dropped the original 3
wrongAnswers.remedy: You had 3 ones before the break. 10 new + 3 old = ?

hints: 50 + something must still equal 63.
Ten new ones join the 3 you already had.

reteach.say: Renaming never changes the number — 50 + 13 is still 63, check it! One ten steps down (60 → 50) and its ten ones join the 3 (3 → 13). Now 13 − 8 works beautifully.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → move up one level; at level 3, interleave break/no-break decisions with across-a-ten items (70 − 23).
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the ten broken slowly on the whiteboard (count all ten new ones), then serve a level-1 item (spot 'not enough ones' or rename after a break).
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one subtraction WITH exchange, one WITHOUT (57 − 23 style), and the child stating when a ten must break → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'two-digit subtraction with exchange'.
struggleProtocol: Go fully concrete — break the ten slowly together, counting the ten new ones as they pour out.
One hint: 'Are there enough ones to take away?'
Re-ask a no-exchange version (48 − 25), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Frame every subtraction as spending or giving away things from LearnerModel.interests (pocket money, game coins, stickers) — never change the numbers or the 'break a ten' language.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish with a subtraction the child can win (no-exchange if needed), then specific process praise: what they DID (checked the ones first, broke a ten instead of flipping, remembered the tens went down) — never 'you're so clever'.

differentiation.support: Model the exchange with blocks before any writing so the flip ('7 − 2 because you can't do 2 − 7') never starts; keep one ten clearly breakable; say 'not enough ones? break a ten' together.
differentiation.stretch: Subtract across a multiple of ten (70 − 23, 80 − 45); estimate first; prove an answer with the add-back check.

extension: 'Break the ten' puzzle — invent one subtraction where you MUST break a ten and one where you don't, then explain to the character what makes them different.
assessmentEvidence: Child solves 2 two-digit subtractions with exchange and one without, breaking a ten correctly (tens reduced by one) and recording the right answers.
revisitLater: A subtraction-with-exchange starter in Lesson 8 (where the inverse will PROVE these answers) and Lesson 12; reappears in money change (Lesson 16).
